rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a story the facts support and a story the founder wishes the facts supported. Its best angle, "Glossier spent a decade as DTC-only. Wholesale is now its fastest-growing channel," is sharp, provable, and honest about the missing channel data. B has real instincts, but "Glossier times its first fragrance launch to its biggest retail push yet" turns concurrence into strategy before the evidence is in, which is how you get a reporter to ask the killing question before paragraph two.
gaps_in_A: Missed a potentially useful fragrance-plus-retail question: it refused "Glossier launches three new fragrance products" correctly, but did not preserve the more interesting angle of whether fragrance needs physical retail sampling.

"The beauty brand born on a blog is coming to Kohl's" needs the Sephora-at-Kohl's split before it is pitchable; A flags that, but the headline still over-centers Kohl's without knowing how much of the expansion is actually Kohl's.

"Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" is viable only with principal access; without that, it is a pleasant company arc, not a story. A admits this, but it is still the softest kept angle.
gaps_in_B: "built on saying no to stores" overstates the fact pattern. The update says DTC-only, not that Glossier publicly rejected stores or built its identity on that refusal.
"covering the 'death of DTC' narrative" drags in a market-wide peg the update does not prove. B later refuses "DTC is dead," then smuggles the same corpse into the kept angle.

"Sephora at Kohl's becomes a test case for prestige beauty in a big-box mall" depends on external trend proof not supplied; as written, Glossier is being used to prove a retail theory the update does not establish.

"Glossier times its first fragrance launch to its biggest retail push yet" is the right question but the wrong headline. "Times" implies causality; the facts only say the fragrance products launch alongside the expansion.
